tagline: Cottonwoods and irrigation canals shape a village beside the Rio Grande
intro: Corrales Road carries NM 448 northeast through Corrales before turning northwest toward Rio Rancho. The village remains rural in character despite its setting between Albuquerque and Rio Rancho, with large stands of cottonwoods west of the Rio Grande. The New Mexico Tourism Department promotes Corrales Road as a scenic byway for its cottonwood forest, acequias and bird habitat.

Corrales formed within the Alameda land grant, awarded to Francisco Montes Vigil in 1710. After subsequent sales, parcels were divided for agriculture and livestock ranching, uses still served by the village’s irrigation canals. The numbered highway has changed at its Albuquerque end: until 2012, NM 448 also included Coors Boulevard between St. Joseph’s Drive and Coors By-Pass. That segment became part of NM 45. In Corrales itself, canals continue to carry Rio Grande water to fields and pastures.

Approaching from Albuquerque, the road is called Coors Road until it crosses into Sandoval County, shortly after the NM 528 intersection at Alameda Boulevard. Continue through the village, with San Ysidro Church on Church Road and the Rio Grande Bosque along Corrales’ eastern edge. The highway turns northwest and ends at NM 528 in Rio Rancho.

moments.title: Corrales
moments.text: Corrales means “corrals,” and water still travels from the Rio Grande to its crop fields and pastures through an extensive canal system. Those irrigation works sit alongside another water arrangement: many homes and businesses rely on their own wells because much of the village has no centralized water system. The village’s Pueblo and Hispano acequias are maintained by the Natural Resources Conservation Service and the Middle Rio Grande Conservancy District. The village government was incorporated in 1971. Corrales retains its rural character within the Albuquerque metropolitan area, surrounded by Albuquerque and Rio Rancho.

moments.title: San Ysidro Church
moments.text: San Ysidro’s towers came later than its adobe walls. The one-story church on Church Road was built in 1868; the towers were added in 1929. It is the second of three churches named for Saint Isidore, the patron saint of farmers. The building entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1980.
moments.notice: The adobe church has one story, with towers added in 1929.

moments.title: Corrales Bosque
moments.text: The cottonwood bosque occupies Corrales’ eastern edge beside the Rio Grande. Its 400 acres extend along ten miles of river and provide habitat for more than 180 species of migrating and nesting birds. The New Mexico Tourism Department identifies bird watching as a favorite activity here. Corrales spans two different habitats: the lower riverside ground and drier, sandy shrubland uphill on the river’s west side.
moments.notice: Cottonwood forest follows the Rio Grande along the village’s eastern edge.
